title: Weakness upon weakness
hook: his mother carried him in weakness upon weakness, so thank Me and your parents (31:14)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luqman's advice to his son, and your line was the first advice. Who did you pass your good advice to, and did you start kindly? Day five hundred thirty-four.

The last few weeks of a pregnancy. The back that aches whatever you do. Sleeping propped on pillows. Getting up again and again in the night. Then the birth itself. Then the newborn months, feeding through the night on almost no sleep, while the body is still recovering. In the middle of Luqman's advice to his son, the Qur'an suddenly interrupts, in God's own voice, to say something about exactly that.

Luqman has just told his son not to ascribe partners to God. And then, before his next piece of advice, there are two verses that aren't Luqman's. They're God speaking. We have enjoined on the human being concerning his parents. Pickthall: "His mother beareth him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years". Then: give thanks to Me and to your parents; to Me is the journey's end. Weakness upon weakness, wahnan 'ala wahn. Commentators read it as weakness piled on weakness: the strain of pregnancy getting heavier month by month, then birth, then nursing. The verse sees it. Notice the order of the thanks. To Me, and to your parents. In one breath, gratitude to God and gratitude to the people who carried and raised you are joined. And then, the next verse adds a limit. If your parents strive to make you associate with God what you have no knowledge of, don't obey them. And yet, keep company with them in this world kindly. So even when you disagree with them about the most important thing, the kindness stays. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ underlined the mother's place. In a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim, a man asks who most deserves his good company. Your mother, the Prophet says. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Your father. Some commentators connect the threefold mother to three hardships: carrying, birth, nursing. Not every relationship with a mother is easy, and the verse doesn't say it is. What it asks is that people remember what was carried.
screen: `GOD'S VOICE INSIDE LUQMAN'S.` · `WAHNAN 'ALA WAHN.` · `THANK ME, AND YOUR PARENTS.` · `YOUR MOTHER, THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank your mother, or pray for her. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of your mother, or of whoever mothered you: a grandmother, an aunt, a foster parent, an older sister. Think of one specific thing she carried for you that you probably never thanked her for. A night shift. A school run. A meal she skipped. If she's alive and it's possible, decide how you'll thank her today. If she's gone, or if things are complicated, you can simply hold her in mind kindly. If you pray, you can pray for her. The bell holds the time.
Weakness upon weakness. The Qur'an's words for what a mother carries: pregnancy, birth and nursing, strain piled on strain. Today's word.
Your line: weakness upon weakness. Today, send your mother, or whoever mothered you, one line of thanks, or say a prayer for her. Day five hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims treat kindness to parents, birr al-walidayn, as a major duty that follows directly after the worship of God, and pray for their parents, living or dead.

original.note: Arabic: weakness upon weakness, the mother's burden in 31:14.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to your mom.
what it means: God's own voice names what a mother carries, and joins thanks to Him with thanks to parents, even when they disagree with you.
what a scholar hears: 31:14–15 is a divine parenthesis inside Luqman's speech; wahnan 'ala wahn; and the threefold mother in Bukhari 5971 and Muslim 2548.
